# TLDR 

This is a blog post that summarizes the things I found helpful while going through the various mathematical notation systems and `R` syntax for multilevel models. Some quick takeaways: 

- When you're unsure about the syntax, always check the math specification. That will help reveal which things are varying by intercept vs. varying by slope. 
- If you use `R` (be it `lm`, `lmer`, `glm`, `glmer`, or `brms`), the R formula most closely resembles the **composite notation** 
- I am a firm believer between the relationships between notation and thinking^[See [Kenneth Iverson's writing]() for more details.], and thus I propose all models follow the Gelman & Hill 2005 and tradition of indexing things, especially in hierarchical contexts 
- As a firm believer of the effects of notation on thinking^[See [https://www.eecg.utoronto.ca/~jzhu/csc326/readings/iverson.pdf](https://www.eecg.utoronto.ca/~jzhu/csc326/readings/iverson.pdf) for more], I hope that documenting these changes will be helpful.  
- Given the most recent version of `equitiomatic`, the quickest way to understand the math (for all fitted models, frequentist and bayesian) is to probably see the equation for yourself using the `extract_eq` function. 

:::

For this post we will consider *main effects* only (i.e., no interaction terms).

# What are multi-level models? 

@mcelreath2020statistical page 415: 

> Multilevel models go by many different names, and some statisticians use the same names for different specialized variants, while other use them all interchangeably. The most common synonymns for "multilevel" are HIERARCHICAL and MIXED EFFECTS. The type of parameters that appear in multilevel models are most commonly known as RANDOM EFFECTS, which itself can mean very different things to different analysts and in different contexts. And even the innocent term "level" can mean differeng things to different people. There's really no cure for this swamp of vocabulary aside from demanding a mathematical or algorithmic definition of the model. Otherwise, there will always be ambiguity.

@mcelreath2020statistical footnote 188: 

> I adopt the terminology of @gelman2005analysis, who argues that the common term _random effects_ hardly aids with understanding, for most people. Indeed, it seems to encourage misunderstanding, partly becasue the terms _fixed_ and _random_ mean different things to different statisticians. See pages 20 -- 21 of Gelman's paper. I fully realize, however, that by trying to spread Gelman's alternative jargon, I am essentially spitting into a very strong wind.


# Nested structures 

Often times we encounter data with some hierarchical nature, e.g., students' scores from schools from different districts, etc. Here we will use the data set used by [this chapter by Stef van Buuren in *Flexible Imputation of Missing Data*](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-threeformulations.html). This is data on school performance of grade 8 pupils in Dutch schools. There data were collected by @brandsma1989effects and were used as the primary examples in Chapters 4 and 5 of @snijders2011multilevel. The data contains a mix of both individual/pupil-level measurements and group/school-level measurements. We will concentrate on four variables: 

- `sch`: school number 
- `lpo`: language test post, outcome at pupil level.
- `sex`: sex of pupil (coded `0 - 1`)
- `den`: school denomination, predictor at school level (coded `1 - 4`)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
df <- brandsma %>% select(sch, lpo, sex, den)

# there is NA data so we filter those out 
df <- df %>% na.omit() %>% 
# turn the other columns into factors 
  mutate(sch = as.factor(sch), 
         sex = as.factor(sex), 
         den = as.factor(den))

# df %>% glimpse()
# df %>% summary()
df %>% head(5)
```

We want to create a model that predicts whether the students' performance (`lpo`) is influenced by their (`sex`) and which school they're from. We will start with ... 

## Level Notation 

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Some facts 

- Introduced by @bryk1992hierarchical. 
- Formulates a multilevel model as a **system of two^[or potentailly more] kinds of equations**, one at level-1, and one at level-2
  - following what was introduced by @bryk1992hierarchical, usually use $\beta$ for level-1 coefficients and $\gamma$ for level-2 coefficients 

::: 

$$\begin{align}
\texttt{lpo}_{ij} &= \beta_{0j} + \beta_{1j}\texttt{sex}_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij} \\ 
\beta_{0j} &= \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01} \texttt{den}_j + u_{0j} \\ 
\beta_{1j} &= \gamma_{10} 
\end{align}
$$

where 

- $\texttt{lpo}_{ij}$ is the test score of pupile $i$ in school $j$. 
- $\beta_{0j}$ denotes the fixed intercept for school $j$, and $\beta_{1j}$ denote the intercept of being a student with a particular gender at school $j$. $\epsilon_{ij}$ is the error. 
- Further, $\beta_{0j}$ has a fixed intercept ($\gamma_{00}$, the first 0 denotes that we're dealing with $\beta_0$ instead of $\beta_1$ and the second 0 denotes that this is an intercept instead of a slope), a slope for the effect of being in denomination $j$, and some random variance $u_{0j}$ at the ... level ...? 
- Note here that the subscripts distinguish the level-1 and level-2 variables --- for the first line, we have parameters subscripted by $ij$ while for the later two lines, we only have parameters with $j$ varying. 

## Composite Notation 

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
# Some facts 

- Introduced by @singer1998using 
- "... essentially the presentation used for mixed effects models" 
- "... the model is expressed in a form similar to regression with a complex error structure" 
- $\beta$ represent the average effects of variables that are known as *fixed effects*  
- $u$ represents heterogeneity between the groups, typically called *random effects*  
- In terms of subscripts: 
  - $j$ is denoting variation at the group level 
  - $ij$ is denoting variation at the child level (within group) level 
- closer in structure to the syntax used in SAS, STATA, and R (`nlme`, `lmer`) 
:::

By substituting the level-2 equations into the level-1 equation, we get the following one-line equation: 

$$
\texttt{lpo}_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \texttt{sex}_{ij} + \beta_2 \texttt{den}_j + u_{0j} + \epsilon_{ij} 
$$

It's usually assumed that $u_{0j} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_u^2)$ and $\epsilon_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\epsilon^2)$. Note that $\beta_0 = \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{10}$ from the previous model. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m2 <- lmer(lpo ~ 1 + sex + den + (1 | sch), data = df)
summary(m2)
```

Note that the above notation is the @gelman2007data approach, where $j[i]$ indicates group membership of individual $i$. 

:::

## Matrix Notation 

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
- the best way to express something succinctly 
- "... this simpler form makes it possible to focus on other aspects of the model ... such as estimation, inference, complex covariance structure, model predictions, diagnostics, and missing data." [@scott2013multilevel] 
::: 

The most common notation is as follows: 
$$\mathbf{y} = X \mathbf{\beta} + Z \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{\epsilon}$$ 
where 

- $X_j$ is the **design matrix** for the fixed effects
- $Z_j$ is the design matrix for the **random effects**.  

Still the same model can be written in matrix notation, just as we have seen before with the linear model. A linear mixed model (LMM) is typically written as: 

$$
y_j = X_j \beta + Z_j u_j + \epsilon_j
$$

where $y_j = \texttt{lpo}_j$ is a column vector containing the scores in cluster $j$, where $X_j = (1, \texttt{den}_j, \texttt{sec}_j)$ is the design matrix. 

There are some nice introductions on [this blog](https://stats.oarc.ucla.edu/other/mult-pkg/introduction-to-linear-mixed-models/). 

## Domains and preferences 

- The matrix model formulation is favored among statisticians
- The level notation is common in the social sciences, as they separate the roles of level-1 and level-2 variables, which eases interpretation of the model and error structures 
- The composite formulation covers the middle ground, for its balance between compactness and clarity, and is used by the introductions into the multilevel analysis for applied researchers 
  - I think the Bayesian wind is most similar to this 
- Also more notes: 
  - Most often we use $i$ as the subscript that denotes the individual row in a dataframe, and use $j$ to indicate the index of something of a grouping variable, like maybe school. You also see sometimes $c$ being used as a subscript, for "cluster". 
- “Critically, and as we illustrate by example in later sections of this chapter, how one characterizes the random effects --- as controls in a regression model, as part of the dependent error structure or as error terms in a set of sub-model regressions --- is tied to how one formulates the MLM notationally and to how one interprets results in practice.”
- Gelman notation: "... alternative notation adopted by Gelman and Hill (2007) ... incorporates the group identification using index look-up functions, wherein $j[i]$ (read $j$ of $i$) identifies the group $j$ to which unique index $i$ belongs.
- “Many variations in notation were introduced in the context of specific sets of research questions within disciplines”
- “notation can influence one’s perspective on these components^["these components" are "... variance components, which are the parameters governing the stochastic terms in a model"] (and vice versa).”

## Mixing notations

### Data with an obvious sense of hierarchy 

Let's say you don't know what "unconditional means model" mean^[Here's [more reading](https://uk.sagepub.com/sites/default/files/upm-assets/126451_book_item_126451.pdf) on unconditional mean model], but you see its mathematical equation as the following: 
$$y_{ij} = \beta_0 + u_{0j} + \epsilon_{ij}$$

The model posits that the score of a randomly selected student $i$ in a randomly selected school $j$ can be represented as a sum of: 

- the population mean $\beta_0$ 
- the effect of being in school $j$: $u_{0j}$
- the effect of being a particular student in school $j$: $\epsilon_{ij}$

# Crossed Random Effects 

Let's suppose you're a psycholinguist. You administed some tests to a group of participants, where each participant answerer different item types multiple types. The model is not necessarily "nested" but given that a same participant is sampled multiple times, you can group by individual participants (`Subject`) and you can also group by item types (`Item`). This is the case demonstrated in @barrRandomEffectsStructure2013. Note that $X_i$ is just an indicator variable, of whether the item is type A versus type B (? to be confirmed). 
@barrRandomEffectsStructure2013 provided a handy table for models and their associated `lmer` syntax, which I will recreate: 

| math | `lm`/`lmer` formula | 
| ---- | ------------------- | 
| $Y_{si} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + e_{si}$ | `lm(Y ~ 1 + X)` | 
| $Y_{si} = \beta_0 + S_{0s} + \beta_1 X_i + e_{si}$ | `Y ~ 1 + X + (1 | Subject)` | 
| $Y_{si} = \beta_0 + S_{0s} + (\beta_1 + S_{1s}) X_i + e_{si}$ | `Y ~ 1 + X + (1 + X | Subject)` |
| $Y_{si} = \beta_0 + S_{0s} + I_{0i} + (\beta_1 + S_{1s}) X_i + e_{si}$ | `Y ~ 1 + X + (1 + X | Subject) + (1 | Item)` |
| $Y_{si} = \beta_0 + S_{0s} + \beta_1 X_i + e_{si}$ | `Y ~ 1 + X + (1 | Subject) + (1 | Item)` |
| $Y_{si} = \beta_0 + I_{0i} + (\beta_1 + S_{1s}) X_i + e_{si}$ | `Y ~ 1 + X + (0 + X | Subject) + (1 | Item)` |

Note that the above math notation is not the most conventional. Everything except the last part I don't quite get.

## What's up with all this terminology? 

My mental model of how hierarchical models work is heavily influenced by @mcelreath2020statistical. In his book, McElreath said: 

> I adopt the terminology of @gelman2005analysis, who argues that the common term *random effects* hardly aids with understanding, for most people. Indeed, it seems to encourage misunderstanding, partly because the terms *fixed* and *random effects* mean different things to different statisticians. See pages 20--21 of Gelman's paper. I fully realize, however, that by trying to spread Gelman's alternative jargon, I am essentially splitting into a very strong wind.

The TLDR is that there have been a lot of different definitions of fixed and random effects in different contexts, across different disciplines. Gelman chose to sidestep the overloaded terms and define 

> ... effects (or coefficients) in a multilevel model as *constant* if they are identical for all groups in a population and *varying* if they are allowed to differ from group to group. 

What this implies in terms of how the math notation^[Referring to section 12.1 Notation from @gelman2007data] is that

- Units $i = 1, ..., n$ 
- Outcome measurements $y = (y_1, ..., y_n)$ 
- Regression predictors represented by an $n \times k$ matrix $X$ 
- Groups $j = 1, ..., J$. This works for a single level of grouping (e.g., students within schools, persons within states, tadpoles within tanks)
  - Occasioally use $k = 1, ..., K$ for a second level of grouping (e.g., students within schools within districts)
- Index variable $j[i]$ code group membership. For example, if you get $j[35] = 4$ that means the 35th data unit in the data belongs to group 4. 

:::





## Math notation and design formula 

According to @mcelreath2020statistical, it is a compact form of notation, that are intimately related to a "common matrix algebra description of linear models".  

[Xiaoying Pu](https://xiaoyingpu.github.io/) provided a [cheat sheet](https://xiaoyingpu.github.io/note/cheat/) for reading/writing R formulas used in `lmer` and `brms`. 

In @barrRandomEffectsStructure2013, the provide a nice table. 

In @gaSoftwareFittingMultilevel2013, they looked at the software for fitting multilevel models, and they had a nice table^[Table 26.1] about statistical software packages containing modules/functions designed to fix various classes of mixed-effects models.
